mcqs.question:
A
Save
has an onclick handler. What is still missing for keyboard and screen-reader users?
options: Nothing: the role makes it a real button for assistive technology.
It is not focusable and does not activate with Enter or Space; that behavior must be added by hand, or the div replaced with a native <button>.
Only an aria-label that describes the action.
Only CSS that makes it look pressed when clicked.
mcqs.explanation: The role changes only the accessibility-tree mapping; it adds no behavior, so the control has no tab stop and no Enter or Space activation. A native <button> supplies keyboard activation, focusability, and its role for free, which is why native HTML is the default. The strongest distractor is option 0: it reflects the common belief that ARIA roles bring the element's behavior with them, when in fact users get a control they can hear but cannot operate.

mcqs.question: A search field ships as `<input type="search" name="q" placeholder="Search products">` with no `<label>` and no ARIA naming. The accessibility inspector still shows `Search products` as the computed name. Which statement is accurate?
options: The name is programmatically determinable, so 4.1.2 is satisfied and the field needs no further labelling.

The placeholder is a hint, not a label: it disappears as soon as the field has text, is painted at reduced contrast, and screen readers do not announce it by default; add a persistent `<label for>` (visually hidden if the design needs it).
The only real defect is 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum); darkening the placeholder text fixes the field.
Nothing is wrong: placeholders are the modern replacement for labels and are announced by screen readers as the field name.
mcqs.explanation: The placeholder fallback in the accessible-name computation is real, which is exactly why the inspector shows a name — but a fallback name is not a label. MDN states that screen readers do not announce placeholder content by default while they do announce label content, that placeholder text is rendered at lower contrast, and that it disappears once the field has a value, so the field loses its identity mid-task (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/placeholder). WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions expects a label or instruction, and 1.3.1 expects the label to be programmatically associated with the control (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#labels-or-instructions). The strongest distractor is option 0: it is the argument an engineer makes after reading the accessibility tree, and it confuses "a name exists" with "the field is labelled for the person filling it". Option 2 isolates one genuine symptom but darkening the text does nothing about the vanishing identity, and option 3 inverts how screen readers treat placeholders.

mcqs.question: aria-hidden="true" is set on a container that includes a button that is still focusable. What do keyboard screen-reader users experience?
options: The button is removed from the tab order along with the accessibility tree
The button is still in the tab order but is exposed with no name or role: a silent tab stop
The container is hidden from the accessibility tree, but the button inside keeps its name and role
The button disappears visually as well
mcqs.explanation: aria-hidden removes content from the accessibility tree but does not remove focusability, so a focusable element inside a hidden subtree stays keyboard-reachable while announcing nothing; MDN documents hiding focused or focusable elements this way as an anti-pattern (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-hidden). The fix is to keep the control outside the hidden subtree or hide it with hidden or display: none, which removes it from the tab order too. The strongest distractor is option 2: the button is inside the hidden subtree, so its name and role are stripped along with the container.

mcqs.question: What does tabindex="-1" do?
options: Removes the element from all focus, including programmatic focus
Adds the element to the tab order before all other controls
Makes the element programmatically focusable, for example with focus() after a route change, without adding it to the sequential tab order
Behaves exactly like tabindex="0"
mcqs.explanation: A value of negative one permits programmatic focus without adding a tab stop, which is the standard tool for moving focus to a heading or main region after a route change or dialog interaction. Zero adds the element to the natural order, and positive values create a separate order that is hard to maintain and confusing for users. The strongest distractor is option 1: it swaps the meaning of negative and positive values, the most common tabindex mix-up.

mcqs.question:
Saved.

gets its text replaced after a user action. What announcement behavior does role="status" imply?
options: None: live behavior requires an explicit aria-live attribute
aria-live="off" by default, like the attribute's own default
aria-live="polite" by default: updates are announced without interrupting the user
aria-live="assertive" by default: updates interrupt immediately
mcqs.explanation: The status role carries an implicit aria-live="polite" (with aria-atomic="true"), so concise status updates are announced at the next opportunity rather than interrupting what the user is reading (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Guides/Live_regions). The strongest distractor is option 1: it is true that the aria-live attribute's own default is off, but the role brings its own implicit value, which is why writing the explicit attribute alongside is often redundant.

mcqs.question: A CI gate fails the build on any accessibility-rule violation. The latest report reads `0 violations` across 40 pages, and the release notes claim the site now conforms to WCAG 2.2 AA. Which claim is defensible?
options: Only that the automated rules passed: W3C states no tool alone can determine conformance, and criteria such as 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence, 2.4.3 Focus Order or the quality of alt text need human evaluation with keyboard and a screen reader.
Zero violations does mean conformance, as long as the scanner's rule set covers every level A and AA success criterion.
Manual review is only needed on pages with custom ARIA widgets; native elements are fully covered by the scanner.
The scan also validates focus order, because `tabindex` values are machine-checkable.
mcqs.explanation: An automated audit is a rules engine run over a DOM snapshot: it can assert repeatable facts (a control has a name, an image has an `alt`) but not meaning or sequence. W3C's evaluation guidance says no tool alone can determine conformance and that knowledgeable human evaluation is required (https://www.w3.org/WAI/test-evaluate/), which is why the defensible statement stops at "the automated rules passed". The strongest distractor is option 1: it sounds rigorous because it adds a coverage condition, but covering every criterion with a rule is not the same as evaluating it — no rule decides whether reading order or focus order makes sense, or whether an alt text describes the right thing. Option 2 is false for native markup too: heading structure, reading order and label wording are not ARIA-specific problems. Option 3 confuses checkable `tabindex` values with the resulting order, which only a human walking the page can judge.

mcqs.question: A skip link ships as `.skip-link { display: none; }` with `.skip-link:focus { display: inline-block; }`. What happens for a keyboard user, and what is the fix?
options: It works: the first Tab press reveals the link, and the next Enter follows it.

It never appears: `display: none` removes the element from rendering, the tab order, and the accessibility tree, so it cannot receive focus and the `:focus` rule never applies; keep it rendered but off-screen and bring it into view on focus.
It works only with a screen reader, because assistive technology can still focus elements that CSS hides.
It fails because WCAG 2.2 2.4.1 requires the skip link to be visible at all times, not only on focus.
mcqs.explanation: A non-rendered element cannot receive focus, so the link is unreachable for exactly the users the bypass mechanism exists for. The working pattern keeps the link in the layout (off-screen or clipped) and reveals it on `:focus` / `:focus-visible`, which is what makes the bypass usable (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#focus-visible). 2.4.1 asks for a mechanism to bypass repeated blocks, not for permanent visibility (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#bypass-blocks). The strongest distractor is option 0: it assumes `:focus` can reveal a `display: none` element, but the element is out of the tab order before any focus state can exist. Option 2 is false as well, since hiding with CSS prunes content from the accessibility tree too, and option 3 over-reads the criterion.

mcqs.question: A signup form marks required fields by rendering the label text in red (#c62828 on white, about 6.4:1) and adding `aria-required="true"` to the input. Nothing else marks those fields. What is the accurate verdict?
options: It passes both criteria: 6.4:1 clears the 4.5:1 minimum for normal text, so the requirement is communicated.
It fails Contrast (Minimum), because normal text needs 7:1 to conform at AA.
Contrast passes, but Use of Color fails: redness is the only visual cue for a sighted user with a color-vision deficiency, and `aria-required` is not a visual cue; add visible text or another marker.
It passes Use of Color, because `aria-required` exposes the required state to assistive technology.
mcqs.explanation: The two rules answer different questions. 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) is about legibility, and 6.4:1 clears its 4.5:1 threshold for normal text (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#contrast-minimum). 1.4.1 Use of Color is about meaning: if red is the only visual difference, the information is unavailable to people who cannot distinguish it, so a non-color marker such as the word "required" or an icon is needed (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#use-of-color). The strongest distractor is option 3: it treats an assistive-technology attribute as if it satisfied a visual criterion, and 1.4.1 explicitly targets users who see the page but not the color. Option 1 confuses AA with AAA (7:1 is 1.4.6), and option 0 stops at the contrast number and misses that meaning is a separate criterion.

mcqs.question: This markup pairs a toggle with a hidden panel. The accessibility inspector shows a button named "Filters" in a collapsed state and no filter nodes at all. Which explanation matches the difference between the DOM and the accessibility tree?
options: `hidden` removes the panel's subtree from the accessibility tree; `aria-controls` records a relationship to it but does not expose or reveal its nodes.
`aria-controls` is what hides the panel until `aria-expanded` becomes true, which is why the nodes are absent from the tree.
The panel is present in the tree as a collapsed region; the inspector only lists nodes that are currently rendered on screen.
The button loses its collapsed state from the tree because the element it controls is hidden, so only its name is exposed.
mcqs.explanation: The `hidden` attribute applies `display: none`, so the panel and its descendants are pruned from the accessibility tree even though they still exist in the DOM; that gap between authored markup and exposed semantics is the whole reason to inspect the tree (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#name-role-value). `aria-controls` only declares a relationship; it is not a reveal mechanism and it does not surface pruned nodes. The strongest distractor is option 2: it blames the inspector's filters, but nothing is being filtered on screen — the browser never exposed the subtree. Option 1 reverses the direction of `aria-controls`, and option 3 invents a dependency between the button's state and the panel's rendering: `aria-expanded` is exposed on the button regardless of whether the panel is currently rendered.

mcqs.question: A product grid is visually reordered with CSS `order` so a promoted item appears first, while in the DOM that item is still last. Every automated rule passes. What will keyboard and screen-reader users actually experience?
options: Screen readers follow the rendered layout, so they announce the visual order; only keyboard users get the DOM order.

Both follow DOM order, so reading and tab sequence run opposite to the visual grid; no rule can judge that the sequence is meaningless, so align source order with the intended order instead of forcing a parallel one.
Adding `tabindex="1"` through `tabindex="9"` to the cards restores the visual order safely for both keyboard and screen-reader users.
An automated scan would flag this as a Meaningful Sequence violation, so it could not pass CI.
mcqs.explanation: Reading order and focus order both come from the DOM, not from visual placement, so reordering with `order` leaves the announced and tabbed sequence out of step with what sighted users see; 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence and 2.4.3 Focus Order are about that sequence (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#meaningful-sequence, https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#focus-order). Automation checks rules, not whether a sequence makes sense, which is exactly the class of bug that survives a clean scan. The strongest distractor is option 2: positive `tabindex` values create a separate, fragile tab order that overrides natural order everywhere else on the page and still leaves reading order untouched. Option 0 assumes assistive technology reads the painted layout, and option 3 assumes a tool can judge meaning.

scenarios.prompt: A design-system toggle shipped after a quick keyboard fix. QA reports: Tab now stops on the control; NVDA announces "switch" with no name; pressing Space flips it and the page also scrolls; pressing Tab or an arrow key while it is focused also flips it; and after a pointer click the control looks on while the screen reader still reports "off". Predict what the accessibility tree exposes for this control, map each symptom to its cause, and write the version you would ship.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Start from the tree, because the tree is what explains the symptoms. The element exposes role `switch`, state `aria-checked="false"`, and it is focusable and in the tab order — that is why Tab reaches it and why the screen reader has something to say. Its accessible name is empty: the only content is two empty spans, so name computation has nothing to use and there is no `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. Note the asymmetry with the plain `<div role="button">` case: here the role is supported and the state is exposed, so the control is announced as a switch that is off and unnamed. The failures are in behavior and state, not in the role mapping.

Map the symptoms one by one. "No name" is the missing programmatic name. "Space flips it and the page scrolls" is a `keydown` handler without `event.preventDefault()`: Space's default action is to scroll, so both happen. "Tab or an arrow key flips it" is a handler that toggles on every keydown instead of only on the activation keys, so moving focus away changes the setting. "Looks on, announces off" is the core defect: the class is the single source of truth for the visual state while `aria-checked` was written once in the markup and never updated, so the tree keeps reporting the initial value — a stale state is worse than no state, because it asserts the opposite of the screen.

The version to ship is native-first, which deletes most of the problem: `<button type="button" role="switch" aria-checked="false" aria-label="Dark mode">` (or `<input type="checkbox" role="switch">` with a `<label>`). A button already provides focusability, activation on Enter and Space with the default scroll suppressed, and the focus ring; `role="switch"` plus `aria-checked` supplies the on/off state; the name comes from visible text or, for an icon-only toggle, from `aria-label`. Keep one state source — the component's `checked` flag — and render both the class and `aria-checked` from it in the same update, so no handler can change one without the other. Style `:focus-visible` explicitly so the indicator survives the reset, and verify with Tab, Space, Enter, the accessibility inspector and a real screen reader, including the moment focus lands and the moment the state changes.
rubric: Predicts the tree correctly: role `switch`, `aria-checked` exposed, focusable, and an empty accessible name — and contrasts it with the generic-div case where the state would be dropped.

Traces all four behavior symptoms to their causes: missing name, unfiltered `keydown`, missing `preventDefault()` for Space, and `aria-checked` never updated because the CSS class is the source of truth.
Ships native-first (button or checkbox with `role="switch"`) rather than adding more key handlers to the div.
Keeps a single state source that updates the visual class and `aria-checked` together, with a programmatic name for an icon-only control.
Verifies with keyboard activation, the accessibility inspector and a screen reader on the state change, not only visually.

scenarios.prompt: This client-side router swaps the view but does nothing else, and keyboard and screen-reader users report that the page 'changes silently'. Design the focus and announcement behavior for route changes, and explain where the logic should live.
scenarios.modelAnswer: A client-rendered route change must do three things deliberately. First, update the document title so the page identity changes for assistive technology and history entries. Second, provide a clear focus destination in the new view: give the new content's primary heading (or the main region) tabindex="-1" and call focus() on it, which moves focus programmatically without inserting a permanent tab stop; this also guarantees focus does not remain on a control that just disappeared. Third, keep normal link semantics and browser history behavior so back, forward, and deep links work, and make sure the new content carries correct headings, landmarks, names, and states. Do not add a generic aria-live 'page loaded' announcement: the title change plus the focused heading is the established, richer signal, and an extra live channel mostly adds noise; announce only what is useful. The implementation belongs in the routing or accessibility platform layer, written once, not repeated per page. Finally, test back and forward navigation, deep links, loading and error states, keyboard traversal, and screen-reader reading order.
rubric: Updates the document title on every route change and can say why it matters.
Moves focus to the new heading or main region using tabindex="-1" and knows why -1 rather than 0.
Rejects a generic aria-live announcement in favor of title plus focus destination, with reasoning.
Places the behavior once in the routing or platform layer instead of duplicating it per page.
Includes testing for back and forward navigation, deep links, and error states with keyboard and a screen reader.

scenarios.prompt: A teammate argues this filter panel is accessible because the ARIA attributes are present. Predict what the accessibility tree exposes for the toggle and for the two size options, list every divergence between the markup and what assistive technology receives, and write the version you would ship.

code.code:
▾ Filters
Size M
Size L

scenarios.modelAnswer:
Start from what the tree contains, not from what the markup declares, because the tree is the contract assistive technology consumes.

**Toggle.** Its computed name is "Filters": the `aria-hidden` icon is excluded from name computation, so the visible text wins. But the node has no widget role — a `div` with `aria-expanded` is a generic element, and `aria-expanded` is not supported there, so the state is dropped. It also has no tab stop and no Enter/Space handling, since only `onclick` is wired. Net effect: a screen-reader user in browse mode meets static text called "Filters" that announces neither "button" nor "collapsed", and a keyboard user cannot reach it at all. `aria-controls` adds nothing user-facing; it declares a relationship, and support for announcing it is inconsistent.

**Panel.** `hidden` applies `display: none`, so the whole subtree is pruned from the tree. The two options do not exist for assistive technology until the panel is shown, and `aria-controls` does not reveal them. That is also why "the attributes are there" is not evidence: the DOM keeps the nodes, the tree does not.

**Size options.** Once the panel is visible, `role="checkbox"` plus text content gives each one a name ("Size M", "Size L") and `aria-checked` gives it a state, so the tree looks roughly right. Three problems remain. They are not focusable (no `tabindex`, and a `div` is not a control), so keyboard users cannot reach or toggle them. Activation is pointer-only: `aria-checked` changes without Enter or Space being handled. And the state is maintained by a hand-written handler, so any other path that changes the visual selection (a "clear all", a server-driven reset) can leave `aria-checked` announcing the opposite of the screen. The `role="group"` wrapper at least gives the set a name, but it is not a substitute for a control contract.

**Fix.** Replace the toggle with a native `<button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="filter-list">Filters</button>` and flip `aria-expanded` and `hidden` in the same update, so the announced state never lags the UI. Replace the option divs with `<fieldset>` + `<legend>` and `<input type="checkbox" id="size-m">` + `<label for="size-m">Size M</label>`; the browser then supplies role, name, state, focusability, and keyboard activation, and the fieldset names the group. If the custom checkbox must stay for design reasons, the minimum contract is `role="checkbox"`, `tabindex="0"`, Enter/Space activation, `aria-checked` updated in every code path, and a group name.

**Verification.** Inspect each node in the accessibility panel for name, role, and state; tab through the panel without a mouse; run the flow with a real screen reader (does it say "Filters, button, collapsed", does expanding keep focus and expose the options?); then run the automated scan as a floor, not as proof — W3C states no tool alone can determine conformance.
rubric: Predicts pruning: the hidden panel contributes no nodes to the accessibility tree, and `aria-controls` is a relationship that neither exposes nor reveals them.
Explains that the toggle has a computed name but no widget role, no tab stop and no keyboard activation, and that `aria-expanded` is not exposed on a generic node.
Identifies that the checkbox roles expose name and state but lack focusability, keyboard activation, and a guaranteed state-sync path, and that the group needs a name.
Ships native elements (button + fieldset/legend + labeled checkboxes, or a complete ARIA contract) with `aria-expanded` and `hidden` updated together.
Verifies through the accessibility inspector, keyboard traversal and a real screen-reader flow, treating a clean automated scan as necessary but not sufficient.
